headline: Nvidia pauses AI server shipments to Southeast Asia amid export compliance review
dek: Nvidia has asked partners including Dell and Super Micro to halt shipments of AI server hardware to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia while U.S. export controls are reviewed, affecting a route that supplies about 24% of China’s AI compute[S1][S2].
what_happened: Nvidia halted AI server shipments to four Southeast Asian nations while reviewing export compliance[S1][S2].

sections.title: Nvidia pauses server shipments to Southeast Asia
paragraphs: Nvidia has asked its manufacturing partners to pause shipments of AI server hardware to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, according to reports on 26 November 2026[S1][S2]. The pause applies to orders from partners such as Dell and Super Micro and is described as an unspecified period while export compliance is reviewed[S1][S2]. The move follows recent U.S. Commerce Department actions to close a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to access Nvidia chips remotely from data centres in those countries[S1][S2].

The Institute for Progress estimates that remote data centres in Southeast Asia provide about 24% of China’s AI computing power, highlighting the significance of the supply route[S1]. Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive days before the halt, but the company has not clarified whether the suspension is temporary or permanent[S2]. The affected partners, including Dell and Super Micro, have told clients that Nvidia is not allowing their server orders to be shipped to the region[S2][S1].

Previously, a gap allowed Chinese companies to rent servers with Nvidia GPUs in Southeast Asian data centres, effectively sidestepping direct export bans[S2]. The recent regulatory change seeks to close that gap, prompting Nvidia to enforce stricter compliance through its supply chain[S1][S2].

sections.title: Kagi launches paid email service with optional AI features
paragraphs: The service emphasizes privacy, ad‑free use, and keyboard shortcuts, and it currently runs only in web browsers[S3]. Native Android and iOS apps are scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2027[S3].

Optional AI features, off by default, let users chat with an agent to search email history, relabel messages at scale, or create new filtering rules[S3]. Pricing options include a $9‑per‑month or $99‑per‑year plan with a 60‑day trial, while the $25‑per‑month Ultimate plan bundles frontier AI models[S3].

Kagi positions the service as a privacy‑focused alternative to Google’s free Gmail, arguing that Google treats users as the product rather than customers[S3]. Google’s own policy, announced on 24 November 2026, will require AI‑driven tools to access Gmail through MCP servers and currently blocks sending email, highlighting the regulatory environment Kagi operates within[S4][S3].

sections.title: SpaceX receives FCC approval for 1 million AI satellites
paragraphs: The Federal Communications Commission gave conditional approval for SpaceX to launch up to 1 million AI chip‑equipped satellites as part of its Starmind initiative[S5][S6][S7]. The agency requires the first satellite to be in orbit by November 2033 and the full constellation by 2040[S5][S6][S7]. The approval follows objections from Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society, which raised concerns about debris and interference[S5][S6][S7].

SpaceX describes Starmind as a solar‑powered orbital data center that will transmit data to Earth via high‑speed lasers linked to Starlink[S5][S6][S7]. The company plans to manufacture the satellite chips at a new Terafab facility[S5][S6][S7]. Critics, including astrophysicist Adam Becker, argue the concept is unrealistic because cooling and energy needs may still be significant[S5][S6][S7]. The FCC dismissed some concerns, stating they fall outside its regulatory authority[S5][S6][S7].

Putting AI compute in space aims to reduce the energy and water consumption of ground data centers[S5][S6][S7]. Several firms, such as Google’s Project Suncatcher and Blue Origin’s planned launch in 2029, are exploring similar concepts[S5][S6][S7]. The FCC’s sign‑off marks the first regulatory green light for a full AI satellite constellation, though opponents warn of orbital congestion and environmental risks[S5][S6][S7].

sections.title: UK regulator seeks joint test of Meta Muse
paragraphs: Meta declined the UK Financial Conduct Authority's request to jointly test its Muse assistant in the regulator's sandbox last week, according to FCA head of innovation Colin Payne[S8]. The FCA wants to see how the tool interacts with consumers and how payments are handled by agents such as Muse[S8].

Payne explained the FCA is working with other UK watchdogs and has been observing AI shopping assistants from firms like Amazon[S8]. He noted that retailers including Sainsbury’s, Marks & Spencer, Ocado, Debenhams Group and Currys have been cooperating with Meta to enable Muse access to their sites[S8]. The FCA is concerned that autonomous agents could prompt unintended actions, especially if consumers do not understand how the AI works, and wants safeguards to protect consumer interests[S8]. Meta spokesperson Matthew Pollard said the company has engaged constructively with regulators and will continue to do so[S8].

Muse, marketed as a personal assistant, launched in September and already has over 10 million users in North America[S8]. British regulators expect similar uptake in the UK because many users already use Meta platforms like Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp[S8].

sections.title: AI models solve most benchmark physics problems
paragraphs: Professor Suvrat Raju at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem he had already solved but not published, using it as a test of AI capability in theoretical physics[S9]. He then organized a private benchmark, TheoPhysEval, by collecting unpublished problems from other physicists that typically take a day for top researchers to solve[S9]. The benchmark was run as AI models improved, culminating in results presented at a September colloquium[S9].

The initial test showed the AI model answered the test problem incorrectly but better than expected, prompting a formal benchmark effort[S9]. When the full set of 50 problems was evaluated, GPT‑6 Astra solved nearly 90 % of them, correctly answering 49 of 50, and even identified errors in the human‑written solutions for the remaining cases[S9]. Each correct answer required less than $3 of compute, comparable to the cost of a coffee in Paris, and was generated after a single human prompt[S9].

Large language models are trained on internet text, so they may have memorized solutions to publicly discussed problems, making unseen, private problems a stricter test of genuine reasoning ability[S9]. TheoPhysEval was designed to avoid this by using problems that had never appeared online, ensuring the AI had to reason rather than recall[S9]. The rapid saturation of the benchmark highlights how quickly AI can reach high performance on specialized scientific tasks[S9].
